speaker: Other
text: This is Supreme Court case number CBA20-008, Joaquin V. Leon Guerrero, individually and as a taxpayer, plaintiff appellant versus government of Guam, department of administration, and Edward Byrne in his capacity as director, defendant's appellants. Appearing for the plaintiff appellant is Attorney Braddock J. Huseman. Appearing for the defendant's appellees is Attorney Jordan Lawrence Pallone. The panel consists of Associate Justice Robert J. Torres, Associate Justice Catherine A. Merriman, and Justice Pro Tem John A. Manglonia. Attorney Huseman reserves 10 minutes.

speaker: roberttorres
text: Thank you, Madam Clerk. Attorney Huseman, you may proceed.

speaker: braddockhuesman
text: Good morning, Your Honors. My name is Braddock J. Huseman. I represent Mr. Leon Guerrero. May it please the court. This case began as a simple taxpayer case and has changed into something quite different. Now it is a case that involves this court's jurisdiction, standing, and even the separation of powers. The Superior Court of Guam dismissed Mr. Leon Guerrero's taxpayer suit because he lacked a sufficiently concrete injury to satisfy the injury requirements found in the Article III of the United States Constitution. The Superior Court came to that decision because of this court's opinion in what the briefing papers refer to as the airport case, In re AB Wampat International Airport Authority, a two-year-old case. The Superior Court interpreted a few paragraphs of dicta within the airport case to conclude that in all cases in Guam, courts require a federal Article III standing analysis, particularly as it pertains to injuries. The Superior Court's interpretation, however, is incorrect. The U.S. Constitution does not mandate Article III requirements on the island of Guam, and neither does the Organic Act. In fact, the requirement of an Article III injury in fact, upends literally decades of case law on Guam. Worse, the requirement of an Article III injury in fact, in all cases, as an irreducible minimum, jeopardizes a host of Guam statutes, as well as this court's own original jurisdiction and several opinions rendered there under. Mr. Leon Guerrero asked that this court reverse the Superior Court's decision, that it harmonize its case law, and that it remand the case to the Superior Court for further proceedings. With my time today, I'd like to discuss three main points. First, there is no irreducible minimum of a case or controversy requirement on Guam. Second, is that the Superior Court erred in its interpretation of the airport case. And finally, that if the Superior Court's decision is allowed to stand, if this court does not harmonize its case law, there are catastrophic implications for jurisprudence on Guam. I'd like to discuss my first issue today, that Guam has no irreducible minimum case or controversy requirement. The powers of Guam's government and the limits on those powers are found in two documents, the United States Constitution and the Organic Act. I'm gonna refer to those today as the founding documents. And those founding documents set up a familiar system of government, a tripartite system where the legislature writes the laws, the executive enforces them, and the judiciary interprets them. But within those founding documents are restrictions on each of those branches of government, as well as grants of power. As an example that I think is particularly germane in this case today, is that federal courts are limited in their jurisdiction by Article III of the United States Constitution. It requires a case or controversy. And a case or controversy is an irreducible minimum in the federal system, because it is in the United States Constitution. And so a case or controversy has been interpreted to mean that a case or controversy requires an actual plaintiff who has been injured by a defendant, and that the court can actually redress that injury. And within that sentence are several jurisdictional ideas. One is standing, a plaintiff who has been injured. One is rightness, has that injury occurred, or is it too speculative to be? The court's redressability, mootness, is an issue, moot. And the shorthand we have for all those terms is justiciability. And justiciability, because it is a shorthand for case or, okay. Because it is a shorthand for case or controversy, is found it's an irreducible minimum contained in Article III.

speaker: roberttorres
text: Now, let me ask you this, though. I mean, clearly, I think even in Beneventi v. Titano, we acknowledge that the Organic Act provides no express case or controversy requirement. At least textually, there's not a case or controversy requirement in the Organic Act that's comparable to Article III. And in fact, the Attorney General points out and tries to equate causes of action or causes to case or controversy. But isn't there another source that could be looked to for imposition of the court's minimum standing requirement? I mean, if the legislature can wholesale, expand, modify, or amend our jurisdiction or our standing requirements, doesn't that make the judicial branch subservient to the legislature and violate separation of powers?

speaker: braddockhuesman
text: Okay, I think what you're asking is, is there a way for the, I think I understand your question. Is there a structural argument for a case or controversy within the Organic Act? Is that-

speaker: roberttorres
text: Yeah, relying on separation of powers or even statutorily, you talked about justiciability and 7GCA 3107, which provides that the Supreme Court has authority to review all justiciable controversies, could perceive to be an additional source for the case or controversy requirement that has been laid out or imposition of a minimum standing requirement that was laid out in the airport case.

speaker: braddockhuesman
text: Sure, Your Honor. Well, and I would say this, that the, so there isn't a separation of powers issue to address that, firstly. And the reason there isn't is there are checks and balances. And so if you look to the federal constitution, there are original grants of jurisdiction, just like there are in the Organic Act to our local courts. And as far back as Mayberry versus Madison, it's been established that if those requirements are in the founding documents, if the original jurisdiction of the United States Supreme Court is enunciated in Article III, that Congress can't amend that original jurisdiction. But if you look at Article III of the United States constitution, it does allow for the Congress to manipulate the appellate jurisdiction of the United States Supreme Court. That is explicitly granted. And in the same way, the jurisdiction of Guam courts can be modified by the legislature with some caveats. So the legislature obviously could never go against the Organic Act or the United States constitution. So in this case, the Organic Act puts some cases solely within the purview of the United States district court for the district of Guam. And obviously the legislature could not expand the jurisdiction there, but the legislature can and does routinely modify this court's jurisdiction. As an example, this court's original jurisdiction, it removes the case or controversy requirement immediately. If the court looks at the court's own enabling statute under its original jurisdiction, the certified question jurisdiction, the legislature says that these don't qualify as cases or controversies, that these are important issues and that the legislature and the governor need them settled and cannot wait for a case or controversy to develop. And so in that case, the legislature has explicitly relaxed the requirement of a case or controversy. In a similar way, if you look at the Open Records Act, the legislature has imposed an Article III requirement on the open records case, because on Guam, unlike in some jurisdictions, the individual who seeks a open record has to be the one that wrote the letter. So in some jurisdictions in the United States, if I, as an attorney, write a letter for a client of mine, but don't name the client and demand documents, my client cannot bring the case. In Guam, however, that's the case in Guam. In some cases, in some jurisdictions, they can, it's not a problem. So the Guam legislature has put the requirement of an injury into our Open Records Act. But generally, the legislature is silent on justiciability. And this court is free to use those prudential concerns anytime it wants. And so I don't think that there is a irreducible minimum that can be found in the constitution, obviously, because it doesn't apply, as this court has said. I don't think the Organic Act can be read to contain such a case or controversy requirement. I don't think there is a separation of powers issues. I think the legislature usually has control over the jurisdiction of the courts they oversee. As long as those, as long as the pronouncements do not run afoul of the founding documents.

speaker: braddockhuesman
text: Well, I think the airport case, AB Wompat, actually says that they were, but should not be thought of as distinct injuries going forward. And I agree with your honor. And so Mr. Leon Guerrero, it isn't important to him that how his claim goes forward. speaker: johnmanglona
text: That's what the court said in the airport case. The legislature can broaden it to elevate de facto to the article, to concrete injury. That was the holding the airport case. But now you're changing your position that we should not overrule the airport case if we can harmonize the injury.

speaker: braddockhuesman
text: With respect, I have not changed my position. I think that the airport case calls for Article III standing. speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: Good morning, Chief Justice, and may it please the court. My name is Jordan Pauloon and I represent the Government of Guam and the Department of Administration, including Director Edward Vernon, his official capacity in this case. We asked this court to affirm the ruling of the court below for primarily two reasons. First, the reason decided by the trial court that we agree with is that the Enforcement of Proper Government Spending Act inorganically removes the standing requirement, particularly the requirement of an injury in fact. And then second, the Enforcement of Proper Government Spending Act itself does not authorize taxpayer suits to challenge the organicity of statutes. It is directed towards challenging exclusively executive action and not legislative acts. The biggest fundamental error in this case or in Leon Guerrero's case is that he does not have any particularized or personalized injury that actually impacts him in this instance.

speaker: roberttorres
text: So you think that the taxpayer standing statute has been entirely eviscerated by the airport case?

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: I don't believe that it's necessarily been entirely eviscerated by the airport case. For example, I think-

speaker: roberttorres
text: Why couldn't the standing that's created under the taxpayer lawsuit, Enforcement of Good Government Spending Act or Proper Government Spending Act provide or elevate the, and impart a judicially cognizable injury where it otherwise might've been inadequate previously?

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: So the legislature can certainly recognize individual rights that were commonly seen in common law as inadequate to bring an action in court. However, in bringing an action in court, you still have to show that you have been injured as a result of whatever it is, that not just that there's a statutory violation, but that you've been injured. And I think this court's opinion in the airport case actually demonstrates that interplay very well. Historically at common law, there was not a right to access certain documents or records held by government agencies. However, the government of Guam and other governments throughout the United States have adopted things such as the Open Government Law Sunshine Act request to give people that right. But in order to actually bring a cause of action, you have to show that you had personally made a request for that information and that information was withheld from you. And so you have been injured in that particular context by the actual withholding of the information that you were otherwise entitled to only under the statute. And so you still have to show the particularized harm there. In this particular instance, there are parties that may be able to show a particularized harm or allegation of harm from the statute in question, such as other insurance companies that are allegedly iced out of the market as a result of this law. However, plaintiff Leon Guerrero does not have any particularized harm directed towards him in any way. He hasn't alleged that he is covered by this law, that he's involved in the insurance market, that he wants to bid on this. He's alleged no other standing than merely he's a taxpayer, which is insufficient under the airport case. And so I think-

speaker: roberttorres
text: Would a retiree or a current Guam employee have standing under this provision?

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: I have not studied that in any particular detail to actually find one way or the other, but I think that that at least alleges something that you could then get into the sufficiency of that harm and whether it's an actual harm or not. Merely a statutory violation alone, even if you're in the zone of interest of the statute, won't necessarily inflict an injury upon you, but there may be questions for somebody impacted by the law that may have standing in that particular instance. They would still have to show a particularized injury, but at least they're getting a little bit closer.

speaker: roberttorres
text: Now, what about the source of establishing the irreducible minimum that was set forth in the airport? Because there really wasn't much discussion other than the reference to Article 3 of the authority for imposing these minimum standing requirements. And clearly the text of the Organic Act or the Omnibus Territories Act either doesn't refer to an injury requirement and doesn't have that case or controversy language. It has causes, as you pointed out. And I know you tried to bootstrap the limited jurisdiction of the district court and the interplay between the local executive and legislative branches as suggesting that maybe that was why Congress wanted to impose the same requirements. But, I mean, clearly Congress knows how to impose those requirements if it wanted to impose those requirements.

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: Certainly, and I don't suggest that any one of those facts, either the text structure or history alone necessarily are this smoking gun of interpretation, but I think when taken together, they are suggestive of that fact. I think more fundamentally is, yeah, I can see that Congress in adopting the Organic Act did not use the words case or controversy, they used the word causes. Because we are dealing in Guam having local courts like in any other territory, you're dealing with things that would by and large fall outside of federal question in a number of circumstances. And mimic what is more usually thought of as state law questions, but would still need to be dealt with by some court in the territory. However, causes of action, that term as historically defined in common law, as recognized in Bikes Dictionary and other cases, still requires that a person be injured by something before they show up in court. Otherwise, the judiciary just gets into the business of issuing advisory opinions on a whole host of statutes, policy issues, and other things. The judiciary by its nature and by the long history of separation of powers cases in Guam and standing cases that were recited in the airport case, has recognized that the judiciary still comes in to decide like actual controversies and cases where people are actually harmed. Mr. Huseman suggests things like the certified question as something that would be open to attack here too. However, if you look at all of the certified question cases that have ever been decided by the Guam Supreme Court, they come in under a context of a real life dispute between two separate branches of the government. And there's a long history of case law related to standing and institutional injuries, such as a legislative injury or injury to an executive office. There's institutional injuries that can be litigated. And this court has been given original jurisdiction over those types of causes of action. But we have never removed a standing requirement for somebody to come in and challenge the organicity of a legislative act. And so you actually have to show, we have a long history of having to actually show that you've been injured by the complaint of conduct. And I think if you take a look at the airport case itself, paragraph 18, this court recites each, not every case, but a bunch of cases in the long history of the standing requirement where you actually have to have an injury in fact. And what Mr. Leandrero was attempting to do was come in and not allege any injury, just complain about what the legislature's done. The proper remedy for that type of thing is through the political and legislative processes. He can petition the legislature. He can vote for legislative officers. He could run for office, a whole bunch of things. That's how the political process works. There is a political check on these types of decisions as well. If he feels like the government isn't making decisions that he feels are best. However, it doesn't give him, just because he disagrees with the law, it doesn't give him the injury necessary to come to court and have the court then absent some injury, second guess a co-equal branch of government, in this case, the legislature. The judiciary comes in and resolves real causes of action where people have really been injured. It's not to litigate policy choices, absent some sort of legislative policy choices, absent some sort of injury. And I think there's also like-

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: Mr. Powell, now that we know the statute is inorganic or unconstitutional, should we send it back to the Superior Court to see if there is an actual injury? That seems to be, have gone by the wayside here. So has Mr. Leongoro indicated that, there is illegal expenditure going on?

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: So to the extent that there may be an illegal expenditure, still does not give Mr. Leongoro standing. That may go to the sufficiency of his cause of action under a failure to state a claim analysis, but it doesn't mean that he has a particularized or personalized injury, in fact, in this case. I do think that the district court's decision that we're all, that's kind of the elephant in the room in this case, it may come into play in a jurisdictional question of mootness, but I don't think it comes into it on the jurisdictional question of standing alone because irrespective of what the issue is here, Mr. Leongoro does not have any personal interest in the outcome of this litigation. He's complaining about this as a matter of policy, which should be accounted for through the political and legislative checks and processes.

speaker: roberttorres
text: So if the legislature by statute, I mean, you pointed out, I mean, and in the airport case, we recognize that the open government law and the record request law were two examples where they could impart a judicially cognizable injury where to establish an injury in fact. So couldn't the taxpayer statute also establish that injury in fact by having there be an illegal expenditure of money as Justice Merriman indicated, and that can be then traced to the challenge action that was taken by the defendant, which was to pay out the money based on this illegal law and the favorable decision can remedy that injury?

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: I think that confuses the legislative impartment of a new right that was historically not recognized a common law with the injury in fact requirement. They're not perfectly the same because the difference between the Sunshine Act and the open government law, which provided actual right to access that must be violated. The key component of the legislative action there is providing the rights. And then the standing occurs in that right is violated. The enforcement of a proper government spending act confers no new right on an individual. It does not provide a right to information, does not provide a right to access or attend certain government meetings. What it does is just say, you can sue over this. You don't have any new rights beyond what there is. It's just go and sue to enjoin. And also importantly, hold these individuals in some cases personally liable for the unlawful expenditures, which actually kind of goes into the second point of my argument as well, that this is not really the type of suit that is authorized under the enforcement of proper government spending act either. It's really intended toward ferreting out executive misdeeds, not legislative policy choices. If you look at the history of the act itself too, it was adopted at a time when the attorney general was still appointed by the governor. So there's a principal agent problem and actually rooting out unlawful corrupt expenditures. And so it was an attempt at that point in time to remedy that principal agent problem because let's say a government official appropriates money from the government coffers, just writes a check to themselves for whatever reason and takes that money. There's not going to be anyone besides the government itself that's going to have standing to challenge that type of conduct, that type of unlawful spending or appropriation because it would probably rise to a level of criminality and would rise to a level of unlawfulness certainly. And the attorney general's office would be the only ones that would be able to bring that particular type of suit. And so at the time when there was a principal agent problem between the governor and the attorney general, they tried to seek to remedy that a little bit to root out that real corruption here, not relitigate policy choices, but rein in executive conduct that was acting in contravention of explicit statements by the legislature. Legislature did not open itself up to be policed by taxpayers. They opened up exclusively executive action to be targeted by these types of suits. So even if we're going to find some narrow exception here, the Enforcement of Proper Government Spending Act doesn't cover this type of lawsuit where they're trying to litigate the organicity and policy choices of the legislature. The legislature didn't and probably wouldn't have opened themselves, their own acts up to challenges through a taxpayer lawsuit. What we're really concerned with is, instances where we have a clear budget bill, it might say even, you cannot spend any money on this program. And then a government official continues to spend money on that program in direct contravention of an appropriations bill or they're stealing money. That type of direct contradiction of a legislative act is really what's being targeted here, not the ability to challenge the organicity and relitigate policy preferences.

speaker: roberttorres
text: But getting back to Justice Merriman's question, now that there's been a determination that it's been an improper delegation and therefore illegal, and if the money continues to be expended, isn't that then directly what you've indicated that it's akin to, there's a specific command that the money not be spent or not be appropriated and the government official ignores that?

speaker: jordanpauluhn

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: Mr. Powell, did the legislature say that a taxpayer is injured if money is spent illegally?

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: No, they didn't. I can pull up the statute here. I do not believe that that's precisely what was stated in the statute itself. Was that there's an injury here. All they say is that a resident shall have standing to sue the government or any other agency for the purpose of enjoining these unlawful expenditures. They do not raise this to the level of preferring an actual right on taxpayers or any other individual. They just say, you have standing to sue. It's this broad pronouncement that just go in and sue but they do not prefer a particular right to have all of your tax dollars paid only towards lawful programs, for example. They just say, go in and sue if somebody in the executive is violating what we've told them to spend money on.

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: What if the legislature were to pass a law that is from Supreme Court precedent, clearly unconstitutional, maybe to give money to a church. Would a taxpayer then have standing? Because there's, even though the law hasn't been determined to be unconstitutional, clearly it violates the Organic Act.

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: If you're coming within the religion context, however, such as the establishment clause that that would fall on, that a circumstance like that would fall on, even if we're dealing with an Article III standing requirement, there would be standing in those cases because there is a particularized, the United States Supreme Court has found a particularized injury in those things because you were essentially being forced to engage in religious activity. And so, some courts view it as, some federal courts view that as a exception to the taxpayer, the bargains taxpayer standing because of an exception given by the First Amendment, or you can view it as an actual injury in fact of having to participate in a religious activity and stand by, depending on the nature of the harm, either offended by a religious thing that's being constructed, such as a cross on the side of a highway or something else. But if we're dealing with religious things, even Article III would confer standing for those types of suits.

speaker: roberttorres
text: The enforcement of proper government spending also has a separate provision that specifically gives the taxpayer or the resident who has the authority to seek a personal judgment to have standing to pursue the execution and collection of the judgment on behalf of the government of Guam. Do you think that's permissible? Does that create the injury in fact?

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: Go ahead and finish.

speaker: roberttorres
text: No, that you assert is missing this particularized injury?

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: I don't think that that even rises to that level because the collection doesn't even provide any money or anything to the taxpayer themselves. It's on behalf of the government of Guam. The injury still here is to the government, not to the individual taxpayer.

speaker: roberttorres
text: So you think that the language in 7109 that gives the right, or in fact uses the word shall have standing to pursue execution and collection on the judgment is inorganic or exceeds the powers that the legislature has to provide that standing to a taxpayer?

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: Now, under our present discussion, yes. The other form that we haven't necessarily discussed per se are such suits as P-TAM actions, for example, which would allow somebody in like the taxing context to whistleblow on somebody and then collect on behalf of the government. But those suits are also pursued in the name of the government against a particular offending individual. But I also think that given the nature of this type of suit that Mr. Leon Guerrero is pursuing, this idea of personal liability is what makes his policy challenges here that much more disturbing. In this case, he does only pursue the injunctive relief, I think as Mr. Huseman points out in his brief, but that's not actually the only remedy he can seek. There's also, there is this issue of personal liability. And so if you have some agency directors such as Mr. Byrne presented with this thing where the legislature has said, we want you to procure a health insurance contract on these terms, nothing about it is like, even if nothing about it screams on its face that this is some religious violation or other thing, but he has this direct command from the legislature saying, do this. So now he's faced with a housing choice of either executing and doing his legally required job of procuring this health insurance contract, but just in the event that he may be wrong sometime in the future, that some court may believe that this is unconstitutional or inorganic, he stands to face a personal judgment of the amount of this health insurance contract. And that's just, that's an outstanding implication from a suit that's supposed to actually weed out real corruption, not place government officials in this Hobbesian choice of either following the law or not just because they're afraid of a personal judgment based on what are really complex and technical legal questions about organicity and constitutionality. And so it's, I think that goes back to really where this fundamental error is in this case, and that's Mr. Leon Guerrero does not have any particular injury, nor does the statute authorize this type of suit for relief on organicity challenges. It's really targeted at actual unlawful spending. You hold up, if there is going to even be a claim here, to state a claim under this, you really need to hold up an act of legislature and show either that here's an authorization that they're violating, or if it's something that was spent without appropriation, go show that there's no appropriation and hold up the executive spending that's done without an appropriation. It's that type of illegal spending where you're comparing executive conduct to actions of one legislature that is really being targeted here. And that's what actually the Enforcement of Proper Government Spending Act, both on its text and its legislative intent in history, is really targeted at and actually means. It doesn't mean come in and relitigate a legislative action every time you disagree with the legislative choice. Those types of choices should be handled through the political processes, not through an action in court by someone who has no personal interest in the outcome of that litigation.

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: Does the injury have to be capable of calculation? This seems to me the kind of factual scenario where it might be extremely difficult to figure out how much money this costs the government in any legal sense. So is there an also requirement that the injury be particular?

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: I think it needs to be particularized. We don't necessarily need perfection in calculating damages and judgments. Otherwise, we'd probably never be able to resolve any case because certain aspects are a little bit of, take a little bit of educated guessing of sorts. But at the same time, you do need some sort of real interest in it. And I actually think that, the U.S. Supreme Court, in a case that I'm now just thinking about, can't recall the name of it off the top of my head, has found that nominal damages, for example, would be sufficient to pursue a case. But you actually still have to have an actual right in those particular instances before you have that injury. But at the same time, the Article III and the federal courts, including the United States Supreme Court, has repeatedly made it clear that you still have to have a personal stake and you actually personally have to be injured. And Guam, through its long history of cases, through the language and history of the Organic Act, has that same requirement that you have to be injured before you appeal to the courts for relief.

speaker: johnmanglona
text: What, Mr. Counsel, what is your response to Leon Guerrero's Virgin Islands case? This is the Donas-Burke, I think, Donas-Stork case? Yes. Yeah, it takes a different position from the Guam Supreme Court in the airport case that there's a case in controversy or case or controversy. What is your precision on that? And it seems that the Organic Act of the Virgin Islands and Guam, the Guam provisions are very similar.

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: The original adoption of the provisions between Guam and the Virgin Islands were similar. Some of the amendments that the person's done, such as the independent election, General's Act for us to transfer powers to our oldest Supreme Court, have not occurred in tandem in the same way. That said as well, just as a matter of jurisprudential concern, there's no special justification or reason to overturn Guam precedent based off of precedent from the Virgin Islands. While it may have some instructive authority here in our interpretive measures, that case hasn't been around since long before Guam's standing jurisprudence developed as recognized by the airport case. And there's no special justification now for departing from that simply because the Virgin Islands had decided it before we had decided on as well. And so it does not offer a special justification. We should follow our own precedent and not that of the Virgin Islands.

speaker: roberttorres
text: The Ninth Circuit also seemed to have reached the same conclusion in the island equipment case,

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: yes. And so the Ninth Circuit has suggested that before as well, but we do have our own judicial autonomy and jurisprudence here that there is, even if this court could have reached a different outcome at an earlier stage of its jurisprudence, there has to be a special justification for deviating from that particular, from the particular case at issue. And I think this also goes to the fundamental problem that Leon Guerrero has advanced on appeal is that he has not proven a special justification for his main ask in this case, which is to overrule a well-reasoned decision of this court based on longstanding prior history of case law. And so for those reasons, we ask this court to affirm the ruling of the court below.

speaker: roberttorres
text: Thank you, Mr. Pallone, you have your time's up. And so how much time does Mr. Huseman have remaining? Courtroom clerk, can you just confirm? He has set four minutes.

speaker: Other
text: Yes, your honor.

speaker: roberttorres
text: All right, four minutes remaining Mr. Huseman to wrap up.

speaker: braddockhuesman
text: All right, your honor. Thank you. I think my friend from the government said the quiet part out loud, which is the government wants to impose article three standing in all cases on Guam. And I think that's a really important point to bring out here. If this court imposes article three, it is the only territory to do so by claiming the Organic Act says it should. Virgin Islands rejects it, the CNMI rejects it up until, well, for 50 years, this court has rejected it. And its predecessors have rejected it. And as far as the reason the government wants-

speaker: roberttorres
text: But there have been other courts that have determined not withstanding the fact that their constitution has no case of controversy requirement to have made a determination that, you know, comparable case of controversy and a minimum that is akin to the federal case of controversy statute is appropriate. And didn't they find their source for imposition of that in separation of powers under their constitution?

speaker: braddockhuesman
text: Not necessarily, your honor. So the government cites Kentucky as one of those jurisdictions. And if you read the Kentucky constitution, it says that the Kentucky courts have jurisdiction over all justiciable causes. It uses the term causes, but it modifies the term causes with justiciability, which goes back to the reason why the government's theory isn't correct. Because justiciability modifies the cause of action, and they are not interchangeable. If they were, the Kentucky constitution could read justiciable justiciables or causes causes. It doesn't make any sense. And so this isn't, and this is a separation of powers-

speaker: roberttorres
text: What about 3107A that talks about justiciable controversies and proceedings?

speaker: braddockhuesman
text: Sure, your honor. And that is your enabling statute as an appeal. And I would wanna brief that for your honor to give you a considered opinion on that. Because that's, now we're talking about Guam law and what that means as far as this court's appellate jurisdiction, right? And if this court's appellate jurisdiction is limited to justiciable claims, but certainly that isn't, that's Guam law, and it isn't the Organic Act. And I wanna be really clear about this. What the government is asking for this court to do is to impose a term that does not exist in the Organic Act. That isn't just a separation of powers issue, right? So the Organic Act says that the courts of Guam shall hear as the law of Guam provides, it's a clear grant of power to the legislature. And what the government is asking for this court to do is not only ignore that grant, but insert other language into the Organic Act. And as we know, the Organic Act isn't drafted by Guam, it's drafted by the US Congress. So at some level, they're asking this court to act as a super legislature on par, not only with, not now on par with the government of Guam, and it's two other branches, but what it says goes. And there isn't a limiting principle here either. Is it just on jurisdiction or is every opinion this court issues a founding document? Because that is what the government is asking for. And I think it is a separation of powers issue, but it goes towards Mr. Leon Guerrero's side, not the government side. I wanna make a quick point about Article Three injuries and the Open Government Act, because this is different than the Open Records Act. As I discussed earlier today, the legislature put in an injury requirement in the Open Records Act, in the Sunshine Act. In the Open Government Act, there is no injury requirement. The people of Guam don't have to show up to a board or a meeting to determine whether the government carried out its duties. And the express intent of the law is to not force the people of Guam to run around to all the different meetings to make sure the government is doing what it's supposed to do. The burden is on the government to carry out open meetings and to do its job right. And the penalty for the government not doing its job right is that anyone can bring a claim to void those actions. Article Three standing is incompatible. Concrete injuries are incompatible with the open records or with the open government law here, just like they're incompatible with the taxpayer claim, but just like they're incompatible with this court's original jurisdiction from the legislature. If Governor Leon Guerrero can bring a certified question that is asking this court for an advisory opinion, and for at least two decades, every time this court issues an advisory opinion, it admits that it's an advisory opinion and that there's no actual standing and the case isn't even ripe yet. But if Governor Leon Guerrero can bring that claim, then Mr. Leon Guerrero can bring that claim. If Mr. Leon Guerrero cannot bring his taxpayer claim, Governor Leon Guerrero cannot have a certified question either. That is the problem with importing Article Three into Guam. It is too blunt an instrument, it just is. And I have very few seconds left, but what I would like to discuss is this idea that this is a policy choice or a dispute on policy, and that could not be further from the truth. The policy arguments have all come from the government today. It's not fair to have a law that allows local Guam government officials to be attacked personally. Well, that's a policy argument. The policy has already been dictated by the legislature. They said, it's okay. I don't know if that's good policy. I don't know if it's bad policy, but it is of course the policy. And individuals have standing to bring these claims. This is not a policy challenge. What Mr. Leon Guerrero wants to do is to remove the procurement authority from the private hospital where it does not belong and place it back with the government where it does. And that injury is no different than an open meetings request. What Mr. Leon Guerrero is asking for, he has a right to have the government expend money legally. The government has illegally delegated authority to a private entity, driving up costs for all of Guam, but expending tax money under that regime is incorrect. And he's asking for that money to stop being spent. This isn't a policy dispute. A policy dispute is an easy resolution. All the government has to do is file a motion to dismiss and say what it did was legal. It didn't do that. It said there was nothing Mr. Leon Guerrero could do about it. And they're here today saying the same thing. Let us act illegally. It's okay. And it isn't okay. And what we're asking for is this court to reverse the superior court, remand the case for further proceedings and to harmonize its case law, to recognize that the legislature can impart injuries, whether that requires a reversal of AB Wompat, I don't think so, but I think those cases can be harmonized. I think the court does need to recognize that the legislature can elevate certain harms to give individual standing. And I'm over my time. If there's no other questions, I'll conclude.

speaker: roberttorres
text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Huseman. Thank you, Mr. Paolun. The court will take the matter under advisement and wish you a written opinion and will now stand adjourned. Thank you very much.
